label: Institution
name: Chaldean Catholic Archdiocese of Salmas
summary:
The Chaldean Catholic Archdiocese of Salmas (Urmia) in northwestern Iran is one of the historical dioceses of the Chaldean Catholic Church — the Eastern Catholic church of the ancient Christian community of Mesopotamia and northwestern Persia, descended from the Church of the East that was divided between those who accepted communion with Rome (Chaldean Catholic Church, formal union from 1552) and those who maintained independence (Assyrian Church of the East).

Salmas (now called Shapur and historically part of Azerbaijan, in northwestern Iran near Lake Urmia) was a major center of Assyrian/Chaldean Christian population before WWI. The Urmia (Lake Urmia) region in northwestern Persia had one of the densest concentrations of Assyrian Christian communities anywhere outside Mesopotamia, including both Chaldean Catholics, Assyrian Church of the East members, and other Christian groups. American Presbyterian missionaries established their largest Persian mission in Urmia from the 1830s.

The Chaldean Catholic community in Salmas was devastated by the Seyfo (Assyrian Genocide) of WWI (1914-1918), during which Ottoman and Kurdish forces killed approximately 250,000-300,000 Assyrian and Chaldean Christians — roughly half the total Assyrian-Chaldean Christian population. The survivors mostly fled to Iraq or the West. The Archdiocese of Salmas today exists primarily as a titular see (a historical diocese without current resident bishop and active congregation) in the Chaldean Catholic Church's jurisdictional structure.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Chaldean Catholic Archdiocese of Salmas — serving the ancient Christian communities of northwestern Persia decimated by the WWI Seyfo Genocide — is historically significant as a monument to the ancient Chaldean Christian civilization of Mesopotamia and Persia and its tragic 20th-century destruction.
